To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) germline mutations in the TP 53 gene account for a substantial fraction of breast cancer/sacroma families, 2) BRCA2 mutations are also present in a fraction of such families, 3) BRCA2 screening should be considered in addition to TP 53 in breast cancer/saccoma families.
the screening of the BRCA2 gene, in addition to the TP53 gene, may be appropriate in families with a breast cancer/sarcomas history, with practical implications.

(1) germline mutations of the TP53 and BR2 genes are responsible for a significant proportion of breast cancer/sarcroma families; and that (2) the screening of BR2, in addition TP53, may improve the identification of the genetic aetiology in such families.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular genetics of cancer.
the genetic aetiology underlying familial aggregations of cancer.
the study of the genetic aetiology and the clinical management of familial aggregations, with a particular focus on breast cancer and soft tissue sarcomas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the TP53 gene accounts for a small fraction of the genetic aetiology in breast cancer/sacroma families.
TP53 mutations are the most frequent cause of LFS, while BRCA2 mutations are the most likely genetic cause of LFL and HBOC.
TP53 and BRCa2 are the two most important genes in breast cancer and sarcoma families, but that the role of BRCA1 remains unclear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the TP53 gene is involved in 13% of breast cancer and soft tissue sarcomas, and that the BRCA2 gene is implicated in 13% (3/23) of breast cancer and 22% (2/9) of soft tissue sarcoma families.
TP53 and BRAC2 mutations are found in about 20% of families with breast cancer and sarcoma, with a higher incidence in LFS and LFL families.
TP53 mutations are present in a small proportion of families with breast cancer and sarcoma, but not in families with only one case of breast or ovarian cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the screening of TP53 and/or BRCA2 genes may be useful to identify families at risk for the development of breast cancer and/or sarcomas.

the screening of both BRCA2 and TP53 is warranted in families with breast cancer/sarcomas, as it can provide important information on the genetic basis of the disease and its implications for the clinical management of the patients and their relatives.
BRCA2 testing should be performed in all families that meet criteria for Li-Fraumenis-like syndrome (LFL) or HBOC syndrome, regardless of whether TP53 testing was positive or negative.
